part_title: AI Fundamentals — From Everyday Examples to Generative AI
review_basis: Reviewed original AIF M01 WebP slides 01–06 individually: foundational AI categories, spam training/inference, timeline, use cases, invoice pipeline and nested AI concepts.

scenes.title: What is artificial intelligence?
scenes.narration: When people hear artificial intelligence, they often imagine a human-like robot. But AI is a much broader idea. Look at the definition beneath the title: AI enables computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence. We can understand that through the three panels, starting on the left. Perceive means recognizing something from the world, like identifying the dog in the photograph. A computer sees pixels, which are tiny colored points in an image. An AI system can analyze patterns in those pixels and recognize a dog rather than just a collection of colors. The middle panel is Understand, where a document and speech bubble represent extracting meaning from language. For example, reading a student's question, 'When is the application deadline?', and identifying what information they need. On the right, Decide means selecting an action toward a goal. Now follow the example at the bottom: a customer sends a message saying 'Can't log in to my account'. The system classifies the message and routes it to a team, such as account support. Classification means assigning an input to one of several categories. It is different from generating a new essay. A system might use rules that a person wrote, or machine learning that learned from past messages. The golden sentence at the bottom is essential: machine learning is ONE way to build AI. Not every AI system learns automatically, and not every AI task requires a chatbot. For a simple test, imagine sorting emails into 'billing', 'login' and 'technical help'. Which task is this? It is classification and routing. Before discussing models, ask what input comes in and what result is needed.

scenes.title: How a learning-based AI system works
scenes.narration: This diagram has two horizontal stages. The top is Training, where a computer learns from examples. The bottom is Inference, where the trained system handles new information. Let's walk through training first. On the far left are examples of emails already labeled 'spam' or 'not spam'. A label is the correct answer attached to a training example. For instance, a suspicious prize message may be marked spam, while an ordinary meeting invitation may be marked not spam. Those labeled examples pass through a training algorithm. An algorithm is a sequence of steps a computer follows. During training, it adjusts the model so that patterns in the examples help separate the two categories. The model is the resulting system, ready to be used with new messages. Look at the bottom row. Here a new email says 'Fifty percent off, just for you'. It has no answer label yet. The trained model analyzes it and predicts 'likely spam' with an illustrated confidence of ninety-six percent. This use of the model is called inference. Inference happens each time a new message is checked; it does not normally mean retraining the model for that message. Notice that ninety-six percent is a confidence score, not a guarantee. The model could mistakenly flag a genuine discount from a shop you trust, or fail to catch a sophisticated scam. That is why the warning at the bottom says a prediction can be wrong. Evaluating a model means testing predictions against reliable answers using data it did not learn from during training. A practical question: when your email app decides whether an incoming message is spam, is it training or inference? It is inference, because it is applying a trained pattern to a new message.

scenes.title: How AI evolved
scenes.narration: This timeline helps explain why AI is not a brand-new idea. At the left, Alan Turing's work around 1950 asked important questions about whether machines could demonstrate intelligent behavior. In 1956, researchers at the Dartmouth workshop helped establish artificial intelligence as a named field. Moving right, expert systems in the nineteen seventies used explicit human-written rules. An example is a medical reasoning program that followed conditions like 'if this symptom is present, then consider this possibility'. Expert systems are limited by the knowledge and rules supplied to them. During the nineteen nineties, machine learning and data mining became more important. Instead of having a developer write every rule, a system could learn useful patterns from examples. In 1997, IBM Deep Blue defeated chess champion Garry Kasparov, showing impressive ability in a specific complex game. In the twenty tens, deep learning advanced. Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers; you can think of these as systems that gradually learn more complicated representations of data. The slide highlights AlphaGo's 2016 victory in Go and the growth of image, audio and language applications. Today AI is used in support assistants, healthcare tools, vehicles and many other areas, with serious responsibilities around safety and fairness. Below the timeline are three approaches: rules, machine learning and deep learning. The medical example shows how a simple fever rule, a system trained on patient data, and image recognition from an X-ray address different tasks. This is NOT a claim that these systems can diagnose patients independently; clinicians must interpret such results and handle medical decisions. The main lesson is that newer techniques do not automatically replace older ones. If a university rule says students must submit an application by a fixed date, a simple rule may be more reliable than asking a generative model to guess the deadline.

scenes.title: AI use cases: identify the task
scenes.narration: This slide groups real-world AI applications into four big categories. Start with Perception on the left. Perception is using information from the physical world, such as images, sounds and sensor readings. The audio example shows someone speaking Spanish and an application turning speech into written text before translating it. AWS provides Amazon Transcribe for speech-to-text and Amazon Translate for language translation. These are different steps. An aircraft or car assistance system also processes information about its surroundings, but safety-critical control requires rigorous engineering and human oversight. The second column is Language. Speech recognition turns spoken words into text; speech generation does the opposite, turning text into natural-sounding audio. Amazon Polly is an AWS text-to-speech service. The third column, Prediction, uses patterns in data to estimate a likely outcome. It includes fraud alerts and tools that help clinicians review images. A prediction of possible pneumonia is NOT a doctor making a confirmed diagnosis. The fourth column is Action. Here AI contributes to doing something: playing a game, proposing code, or helping automate a business process. The important distinction is that generating a suggestion is not the same as safely performing a privileged action. Applications still need permissions and checks. Follow the worked example at the bottom: a Spanish-speaking customer calls, the application first transcribes the sound into Spanish text, then translates it into English. The two AWS services solve different parts of the request. Let's practice: if the requirement is to speak an English sentence aloud, would we choose Translate or Polly? Polly, because the task is text-to-speech. If the requirement is to turn spoken Spanish into English text, we would combine transcription and translation. First recognize the task; then select the capability.

scenes.title: Intelligent document processing
scenes.narration: Imagine an accounts department receiving a PDF invoice. The invoice contains seller and buyer names, item descriptions, quantities, prices and totals. The company wants those details in a database without an employee typing every field. The slide walks through five numbered stages, and each has a different responsibility. Step one, Input document: the scanned PDF is stored in Amazon S3. S3 is AWS object storage, which means it holds files or other objects so applications can retrieve them. Step two, Extraction: Amazon Textract examines the document image and detects printed text, forms, key-value pairs and tables. A key-value pair might be 'Invoice number' followed by 'INV-1001'. Step three, Interpretation: application logic or language processing helps understand which extracted text is the seller, buyer or line item. NLP stands for natural language processing, the study and use of computers working with human language. Step four, Validation: check that required fields exist and that arithmetic agrees. Look at the sample line item: four wireless mice cost ten dollars each. Four times ten equals forty dollars. The application should compare the extracted total with that calculation. If a seller name is absent, handwriting is unclear, or totals disagree, the system should request human review instead of silently storing an incorrect invoice. Step five, Storage: approved structured records are written to Amazon DynamoDB, a managed database for records that an application can query. The JSON-like result at the bottom is simply structured key-and-value information, not a magical new invoice. Notice that S3, Textract, validation logic, human review and DynamoDB perform different jobs. A real implementation can use other services, but the architecture illustrates the principle. Ask yourself: if Textract recognizes a price with high confidence, can we skip checking that the invoice total adds up? No. Confidence in text recognition is separate from the business rule that the amount must be correct.

scenes.title: AI, machine learning and generative AI
scenes.narration: The nested shapes here answer one of the most common beginner questions. Why do people say artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI as though they mean the same thing? They are related, but they are not interchangeable labels. Start with the largest outer shape: artificial intelligence is the broad field of systems that perform intelligent tasks. Some use explicit rules. Inside that is machine learning, where a system learns useful patterns from data instead of relying entirely on rules written by people. Inside machine learning is deep learning, which commonly uses multi-layer neural networks to find complex patterns. Inside the illustration is generative AI, which creates new content from patterns learned during training. Many modern generative systems use deep learning, although the broader category of generative modeling has a longer history and different techniques. The examples on the right make the distinctions clear. An expert-system rule is an AI approach that need not use machine learning. Predicting whether a customer will leave a subscription is a machine-learning prediction task. Recognizing objects in complicated images is a common deep-learning task. Writing a new product description is a generative-AI task. A generative model does not have human understanding or a guarantee of correctness simply because its answer sounds natural. Evaluate generated information for accuracy, privacy and safety before using it. Here's the exam-style decision. A retailer wants a system to predict next month's demand from past sales. Is that primarily generative AI? No; it is a prediction problem often suited to conventional machine learning. If the same retailer wants a first draft of marketing copy, that's a generative task. The difference is the output the business actually needs. As we move into AWS cloud foundations, we will connect each problem type to an appropriate way of delivering the solution.
